summary: This document defines a methodology for auditing Docusaurus blog articles to ensure readers encounter proof-of-value quickly rather than prerequisites or theory first. It establishes four mechanical passes (position-based metrics, repetition detection, author-journey noise, and a 30-second reader test) that produce one of three verdicts: OK (journal only), MINOR (note but no action), or RESTRUCTURE (file a TODO). The audit prioritizes reordering content, not cutting, and treats certain scaffolding like QuickJump components as invisible to measurements.

explanations.39: T represents the line number where `<!-- truncate -->` appears (the article excerpt boundary), and BODY is the total line count of the readable article body after that point — used as the denominator to compute how early proof appears as a percentage.
explanations.42: QuickJump components are navigation aids that sit between the excerpt cutoff and real content; move the truncate marker past them before measuring, because they don't represent install work or proof and shouldn't inflate the body length artificially.
explanations.54: Proof is the first concrete evidence the reader sees that the tool/technique actually works — things like a command output, a result image, or a diagram — not just setup instructions.
explanations.64: If an article never shows a working result, assign 100% TTV to flag that the reader gets no value proof at all, regardless of article length.
explanations.68: The TTV percentage is computed as (line number where proof starts minus line T) divided by total body length; thresholds are green below 15%, yellow 15–30%, red 30% or higher.
explanations.76: Articles often repeat the same core idea multiple times across different sections, making them feel padded; Pass 2 mechanically counts how many times each main claim reappears in the body.
explanations.87: This AWK command splits the article into sections (starting at line T) by heading level 2, then counts words per section so you can see which ones are disproportionately long relative to their content.
explanations.119: This grep pattern finds common phrases that signal the author is narrating their own process of discovery (trial-and-error, surprise, learning the hard way) rather than teaching the reader.
explanations.127: When an author says 'I found out the hard way,' that sentence should be cut because the article already demonstrates the workaround in code — the story adds nothing the reader needs.
explanations.151: A high TTV metric doesn't save an article if the opening paragraph never explains what problem the tool solves; metrics make audits consistent but never override the gut check of whether a reader would keep reading.
